Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN)  -- More than half the Christian population has fled the northern Iraqi city of Mosul in reaction to a campaign of killings and intimidation, according to the United Nations. Christian women attend a religious service Sunday at a church in Baghdad. An estimated 13,000 Christians have left because of oppression the U.S. government blames on al Qaeda in Iraq. Mosul, in Nineveh province, is one of the last Iraqi cities where al Qaeda in Iraq has a significant presence and routinely carries out attacks. An estimated 2,300 families have fled Mosul this month, but the exodus has started to ebb, Nineveh province's Deputy Gov. Khasro Goran said Tuesday. No Christian family has left the city over the past seven days, and at least 100 families returned to their homes in and around Mosul during that time, Goran said. Authorities said they believe Christian demonstrations earlier this month may have prompted the attacks. Hundreds of Christians took to the streets in Mosul and surrounding villages and towns demanding adequate representation on provincial councils, whose members will be chosen in local elections in January. The violence that followed those protests left at least 14 Iraqi Christians dead and prompted the Iraqi government to dispatch more security forces to patrol the city. Violence has declined as a result, Iraqi officials said. Last week, U.S. Defense Department spokesman Geoff Morrell said the anti-Christian attacks and threats are partly "due to elements of al Qaeda that still enjoy some ability to operate up there." "This is an attempt, it appears, to try to inflame tensions and fault lines that exist between religious and sectarian groups," Morrell said. The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees is helping many of the displaced families, most of whom have fled to nearby villages in Nineveh province. About 400 others have crossed into Syria, but many have said they no longer feel safe there, according to the refugee agency. Syria already hosts more than 1 million Iraqi refugees. The U.N. agency said many of the Iraqi Christians told stories of intimidation and death threats. "One woman said she and her mother left Mosul early last week, two days after someone called one of her colleagues at work and said that all Christians should leave the city immediately or be killed," according to a UNHCR news release. "She said she was unnerved but decided to leave only after hearing reports that 11 people had been killed at a checkpoint by militiamen dressed as police officers. She and her mother escaped with a couple of bags and all the money that they had in the house -- they did not dare go to the bank to remove their savings." A nurse told UNHCR that the threats against Christians in Mosul began months ago "with phone calls, letters and messages left on doors." In other violence Tuesday in Mosul, four police officers were killed and four wounded when gunmen opened fire on their vehicle, an Iraqi Interior Ministry official said. Gunmen in cars ambushed police as they were on their way to start work in west Mosul's al-Amil neighborhood, the official said. Also Tuesday in Baghdad, six civilians died and 23 were hurt in four bombings, the official said. In eastern Baghdad, in the Shiite al-Baladiyat neighborhood, a roadside bomb exploded Tuesday afternoon, killing one civilian and wounding five others, the official said. Earlier, a parked car exploded near a busy outdoor market in the western al-Jihad neighborhood, killing at least five people and wounding 11 others, the Interior Ministry official said. No other details were available about the blast. Two roadside bombs exploded in central Baghdad's al-Nahdha commercial area, wounding seven people, the official said. The first blast hurt four civilians, while the second wounded three, the official said. Also Tuesday, the Iraqi army and police discovered 20 decomposed bodies in the basement of an abandoned house in Tal Afar, a town about 43 miles (70 kilometers) west of Mosul. There was no indication of how the victims -- who could not immediately be identified -- were killed, the official said. Authorities discovered the bodies after receiving tips from local residents. CNN's Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed to this report.

BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) — More than half of the Christian population has fled the northern Iraqi city of Mosul in response to a campaign of killings and intimidation, according to the United Nations.

Christian women attended a religious service Sunday at a church in Baghdad. An estimated 13,000 Christians have left Mosul because of oppression that the U.S. government attributes to al Qaeda in Iraq.

Mosul, located in Nineveh province, is one of the last Iraqi cities where al Qaeda in Iraq maintains a significant presence and routinely carries out attacks.

An estimated 2,300 families have fled Mosul this month, though the exodus has begun to subside, Nineveh province’s Deputy Governor Khasro Goran said Tuesday. No Christian families have left the city over the past seven days, and at least 100 families returned to their homes in and around Mosul during that period, Goran said.

Authorities said they believe Christian demonstrations earlier this month may have prompted the attacks. Hundreds of Christians took to the streets in Mosul and in surrounding villages and towns, demanding adequate representation on provincial councils, whose members will be chosen in local elections in January.

The violence that followed those protests left at least 14 Iraqi Christians dead and prompted the Iraqi government to deploy additional security forces to patrol the city. Iraqi officials said violence has declined as a result.

Last week, U.S. Defense Department spokesman Geoff Morrell said the anti-Christian attacks and threats were partly “due to elements of al Qaeda that still enjoy some ability to operate up there.”

“This is an attempt, it appears, to try to inflame tensions and fault lines that exist between religious and sectarian groups,” Morrell said.

The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees is assisting many of the displaced families, most of whom have fled to nearby villages in Nineveh province. About 400 others have crossed into Syria, though many have said they no longer feel safe there, according to the refugee agency. Syria already hosts more than 1 million Iraqi refugees.

The U.N. agency said many Iraqi Christians recounted stories of intimidation and death threats.

“One woman said she and her mother left Mosul early last week, two days after someone called one of her colleagues at work and said that all Christians should leave the city immediately or be killed,” according to a UNHCR news release. “She said she was unnerved but decided to leave only after hearing reports that 11 people had been killed at a checkpoint by militiamen dressed as police officers. She and her mother escaped with a couple of bags and all the money that they had in the house — they did not dare go to the bank to remove their savings.”

A nurse told UNHCR that the threats against Christians in Mosul began months ago “with phone calls, letters and messages left on doors.”

In other violence Tuesday in Mosul, four police officers were killed and four others wounded when gunmen opened fire on their vehicle, an Iraqi Interior Ministry official said. Gunmen in cars ambushed the officers as they were on their way to start work in west Mosul’s al-Amil neighborhood, the official said.

Also Tuesday in Baghdad, six civilians were killed and 23 were injured in four bombings, the official said.

In eastern Baghdad, in the Shiite al-Baladiyat neighborhood, a roadside bomb exploded Tuesday afternoon, killing one civilian and wounding five others, the official said.

Earlier, a parked car exploded near a busy outdoor market in the western al-Jihad neighborhood, killing at least five people and wounding 11 others, the Interior Ministry official said. No further details were available about the blast.

Two roadside bombs exploded in central Baghdad’s al-Nahdha commercial area, wounding seven people, the official said. The first blast injured four civilians, while the second wounded three, the official said.

Also Tuesday, the Iraqi army and police discovered 20 decomposed bodies in the basement of an abandoned house in Tal Afar, a town about 43 miles (70 kilometers) west of Mosul. There was no indication of how the victims — who could not immediately be identified — had been killed, the official said.

Authorities discovered the bodies after receiving tips from local residents.

CNN’s Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed to this report.

On Sunday, Christian women were seen taking part in a church service in Baghdad. Roughly 13,000 Christians have departed Mosul because of persecution that the U.S. government attributes to al Qaeda in Iraq. Mosul, located in Nineveh province, remains one of the few Iraqi cities where al Qaeda in Iraq still maintains a notable foothold and frequently launches attacks.

Nineveh Deputy Governor Khasro Goran said Tuesday that about 2,300 families had left Mosul during the month, though the pace of departures had begun to slow. He said no Christian families had fled in the previous week, while at least 100 families had gone back to their homes in Mosul and nearby areas during that period.

Officials said they suspect the violence may have been triggered by Christian protests earlier in the month. Hundreds of Christians demonstrated in Mosul and nearby villages and towns, calling for fair representation on provincial councils, whose members are to be selected in local elections scheduled for January.

At least 14 Iraqi Christians were killed in the violence that followed the demonstrations. In response, Iraq’s government sent additional security personnel to patrol Mosul. Iraqi officials said the increased security helped reduce the violence.

Geoff Morrell, a spokesman for the U.S. Defense Department, said last week that attacks and threats targeting Christians were partly “due to elements of al Qaeda that still enjoy some ability to operate up there.”

“This is an attempt, it appears, to try to inflame tensions and fault lines that exist between religious and sectarian groups,” Morrell said.

The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees has been assisting many displaced families, most of whom have taken refuge in villages elsewhere in Nineveh province. The agency said around 400 others have entered Syria, though many reported that they no longer feel secure there. Syria is already home to more than 1 million Iraqi refugees.

According to UNHCR, many Iraqi Christians described receiving threats, intimidation and warnings that they could be killed.

“One woman said she and her mother left Mosul early last week, two days after someone called one of her colleagues at work and said that all Christians should leave the city immediately or be killed,” a UNHCR statement said. “She said she was unnerved but decided to leave only after hearing reports that 11 people had been killed at a checkpoint by militiamen dressed as police officers. She and her mother escaped with a couple of bags and all the money that they had in the house -- they did not dare go to the bank to remove their savings.”

A nurse told UNHCR that intimidation of Christians in Mosul had started months earlier through “phone calls, letters and messages left on doors.”

Separately on Tuesday in Mosul, four police officers were killed and four others injured when attackers fired on their vehicle, an Iraqi Interior Ministry official said. The official said gunmen in cars ambushed the officers as they were heading to work in the al-Amil neighborhood of western Mosul.

In Baghdad on Tuesday, six civilians were killed and 23 others wounded in four bomb attacks, the official said.

In eastern Baghdad’s Shiite al-Baladiyat district, a roadside bomb went off Tuesday afternoon, killing one civilian and injuring five more, according to the official. Earlier, a car bomb parked near a crowded open-air market in the western al-Jihad neighborhood killed at least five people and wounded 11 others, the Interior Ministry official said. No further information about that explosion was immediately available.

Two roadside bombs also detonated in the al-Nahdha commercial district in central Baghdad, injuring seven people. The first explosion wounded four civilians, and the second injured three, the official said.

Also Tuesday, Iraqi soldiers and police found 20 decomposed bodies in the basement of an abandoned house in Tal Afar, about 43 miles, or 70 kilometers, west of Mosul. The victims could not immediately be identified, and there was no indication of how they had been killed, the official said. Authorities found the bodies after receiving information from local residents.

CNN’s Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed to the report.

More than half of Mosul’s Christian population fled the northern Iraqi city after a wave of killings, threats, and intimidation blamed on al Qaeda in Iraq, creating one of the most serious recent crises for the country’s Christian minority.

Families left their homes in large numbers after reports that Christians were being targeted in several neighborhoods. Many sought refuge in nearby villages and towns, while others moved in with relatives or took shelter in churches and community centers. The sudden displacement placed pressure on local authorities, aid groups, and religious organizations, which worked to provide food, water, blankets, and other basic assistance.

In response, Iraqi officials sent additional security forces to Mosul in an effort to restore confidence and prevent further attacks. Checkpoints were increased, patrols were expanded in affected areas, and authorities promised to pursue those responsible for the violence. The government’s actions were intended not only to protect those who remained, but also to encourage displaced families to return home.

The United Nations also became involved, assisting families who had fled and assessing their needs. International concern grew as reports emerged of Christians leaving behind homes, businesses, schools, and churches. The displacement underscored the precarious position of religious minorities in Iraq, particularly in areas where militant groups continued to operate despite broader improvements in security.

In recent days, the exodus from Mosul has begun to slow. Some Christian families have started returning to their homes as the level of violence has declined and the presence of security forces has increased. Local leaders have said that the improved security situation has helped ease fears, though many families remain cautious and uncertain about whether it is safe to return permanently.

The crisis in Mosul illustrates both the effect of stronger security measures and the continuing vulnerability of Iraq’s Christian community. While the deployment of additional forces appears to have reduced attacks and encouraged some returns, the flight of so many families shows how quickly fear can spread when minority communities are targeted. For many Christians in Mosul, the decision to return will depend not only on a temporary decline in violence, but on whether they believe they can live safely and freely in the long term.

counterfactuals.output:
**BAGHDAD, Iraq —** Thousands of Iraqi Christians have fled the northern city of Mosul after a wave of killings, threats and intimidation blamed by local officials on al Qaeda-linked militants, according to the U.N. refugee agency and Iraqi authorities.

The exodus has emptied parts of Mosul’s Christian neighborhoods, with families leaving their homes for nearby villages, monasteries and towns in the Nineveh Plain, as well as the Kurdish-controlled areas to the north. Many left with little more than clothing and identification documents after receiving death threats or hearing reports of Christians being singled out at checkpoints and in their homes.

The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees said its teams were monitoring the displacement and working with local authorities and aid groups to provide emergency assistance, including food, blankets, mattresses and basic household supplies. UNHCR officials said the number of displaced families was continuing to rise as fear spread through the community.

Iraqi Christian leaders said the violence appeared designed to force Christians out of Mosul, one of Iraq’s most ethnically and religiously mixed cities. Community representatives reported that several Christians had been killed in separate attacks and that others had received warnings to convert, pay money or leave.

Iraqi security officials blamed the campaign on al Qaeda in Iraq and affiliated extremist groups, which have long targeted religious minorities, government employees, police and civilians in an effort to destabilize the country. Authorities said additional police and army units had been deployed in Mosul and surrounding areas to protect displaced families and investigate the killings.

Mosul, the capital of Nineveh province, has remained one of Iraq’s most volatile cities despite security gains elsewhere in the country. U.S. and Iraqi officials have repeatedly described it as a major remaining stronghold for insurgent networks pushed out of Baghdad, Anbar province and other areas.

The latest intimidation campaign has deepened fears among Iraq’s ancient Christian community, whose numbers have fallen sharply since the 2003 U.S.-led invasion. Churches have been bombed, clergy have been kidnapped or killed, and many Christians have fled to Syria, Jordan, Lebanon and northern Iraq.

UNHCR has warned for years that Iraq’s minorities — including Christians, Yazidis, Shabak and Mandaeans — remain especially vulnerable because they often lack tribal or militia protection. The agency said many displaced Christians from Mosul were staying with relatives or in church-run shelters, while others needed urgent humanitarian support.

The violence in Mosul came as attacks continued elsewhere in Iraq. Police reported bombings, shootings and roadside explosions in several provinces, underscoring the fragile security situation despite a nationwide decline in violence compared with the height of Iraq’s sectarian war.

In Baghdad, security forces continued to face sporadic bomb attacks targeting patrols, government workers and crowded civilian areas. In Diyala province, insurgent activity persisted despite repeated military operations. In northern Iraq, officials said militants remained capable of carrying out assassinations and intimidation campaigns against civilians viewed as vulnerable or politically useful targets.

Iraqi leaders condemned the attacks on Christians and pledged to protect the community. But displaced families said they were afraid to return until those responsible were arrested and security in Mosul improved.

“We left because we were told we would be killed,” one displaced resident said. “We do not know when we can go back — or if we can go back at all.”

counterfactuals.output:
**BAGHDAD, Oct. 13, 2008** — Thousands of Iraqi Christians have fled the northern city of Mosul after a wave of killings, threats and intimidation that community leaders and officials described as one of the most serious assaults on the country’s dwindling Christian minority since the fall of Saddam Hussein.

Iraqi officials, church representatives and aid agencies said more than 1,000 Christian families — and possibly several thousand people — had left Mosul in recent days, many taking refuge in nearby villages, monasteries and towns in the Nineveh plain. The flight followed the killing of a number of Christians in the city and reports that armed men had gone door to door warning families to leave or face death.

The U.N. refugee agency said it was rushing emergency assistance to displaced families, including food, blankets and household supplies.

“This is a very worrying development,” the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees said in a statement issued through officials monitoring northern Iraq. U.N. representatives in Baghdad also condemned the attacks, saying the “deliberate targeting of any religious or ethnic group is unacceptable” and calling on Iraqi authorities to protect civilians and allow displaced families to return safely.

U.S. officials also denounced the violence. The U.S. Embassy in Baghdad said in a statement that it “strongly condemns the recent attacks against Christians in Mosul” and supports the Iraqi government’s efforts to investigate the killings and provide security for threatened communities. American military officials in northern Iraq said they were coordinating with Iraqi security forces, but emphasized that Iraqi police and army units were taking the lead inside the city.

The killings have deepened fears among Iraq’s Christians, whose population has fallen sharply since 2003 because of insurgent violence, kidnappings, church bombings and targeted assassinations. Christians have lived in Iraq for nearly 2,000 years, with large communities historically concentrated in Baghdad, Mosul and towns across Nineveh province.

In Mosul, police said several Christians had been shot dead over the previous two weeks, including men killed at shops, near their homes or while traveling through the city. Local officials said at least 10 to 12 Christians had been killed in the recent campaign, though exact figures varied because many families were too frightened to report threats or deaths publicly. Security forces also reported attacks on Christian homes, including bombings or attempted bombings meant to frighten residents into leaving.

The exodus prompted the Iraqi government to deploy additional police to Christian neighborhoods and set up checkpoints around churches and residential districts. Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki ordered an investigation and sent officials to Nineveh province, while local Christian leaders accused authorities of responding too slowly.

Some displaced families said they left with little more than clothing and identity documents.

“They told us: leave Mosul or you will be killed,” one Christian resident who fled to a village outside the city said. “We cannot go back unless there is real protection.”

The violence in Mosul came as attacks continued elsewhere in Iraq. In Baghdad, police reported separate bombings and shootings that killed and wounded civilians and security personnel. In one incident, a roadside bomb or parked car bomb struck a busy area of the capital, killing several people and wounding others, officials said. Additional attacks in and around Baghdad left more casualties, underscoring the persistent insecurity despite a major decline in nationwide violence compared with the previous year.

Iraqi officials said they were investigating whether the Mosul attacks were carried out by al-Qaida in Iraq or other Sunni extremist groups seeking to destabilize the city, intimidate minorities and embarrass the government. Mosul remained one of the last major urban strongholds for insurgent networks in 2008, even after security operations reduced violence in Baghdad and other parts of the country.

Christian leaders appealed for international attention but said they did not want the crisis to accelerate permanent emigration.

“Our people are terrified,” one church official in northern Iraq said. “They need protection, not just words.”

Aid workers warned that many displaced families were staying in overcrowded homes, churches and community halls. The U.N. said it would continue assessing needs in the Nineveh plain and coordinate relief with Iraqi authorities and local organizations.

The attacks have raised broader questions about the future of Iraq’s minorities — including Christians, Yazidis, Shabak and others — in disputed and volatile areas of the north. For many Christians who fled Mosul, the immediate concern was simpler: whether the city that had been home to their families for generations could ever be safe again.

MOSUL, Iraq — Thousands of Christian families have fled the northern Iraqi city of Mosul after a wave of killings, threats and intimidation that community leaders and officials say has spread fear through one of Iraq’s oldest Christian populations.

The exodus has unfolded over days amid reports that gunmen ordered Christians to leave the city, convert, pay protection money or face death. Several Christians have been killed in targeted attacks, and many families have abandoned homes, shops and churches for nearby Christian towns, villages and monasteries in Nineveh province, as well as for the Kurdish-administered region farther north.

Iraqi authorities have blamed extremist groups, including al Qaeda in Iraq, for the campaign. The organization, though weakened by U.S. and Iraqi military operations and the rise of Sunni tribal “Awakening” forces, has remained active in Mosul and surrounding areas, exploiting ethnic, religious and political tensions in one of the country’s most contested regions.

Mosul, Iraq’s third-largest city, has long been considered one of the last major urban strongholds for al Qaeda in Iraq and other insurgent networks. Its mixed population — including Sunni Arabs, Kurds, Turkmen, Yazidis, Shabaks and Christians — has made the city a flashpoint in disputes over authority, security and identity. Christians, who generally have little militia protection and are not aligned with powerful armed factions, have been especially vulnerable.

Local Christian leaders said families began leaving after a series of assassinations and threats targeting members of the community. Some residents said leaflets and verbal warnings spread through Christian neighborhoods, while others described gunmen approaching homes or businesses. Panic grew as word circulated that Christians were being singled out because of their faith.

Many of those fleeing have taken shelter in towns such as Qaraqosh, Bartella and Karamles, areas with large Christian populations east and southeast of Mosul. Churches and aid groups have provided temporary housing, food and blankets, while some families have stayed with relatives. Others have crossed into the relatively safer Kurdish region, where tens of thousands of Christians had already sought refuge during earlier years of Iraq’s sectarian violence.

The displacement has renewed concern over the future of Iraq’s Christian minority, one of the oldest in the Middle East. Before the 2003 U.S.-led invasion, Iraq was home to an estimated 1 million or more Christians, including Chaldean Catholics, Assyrians, Syriac Catholics and Syriac Orthodox communities. Years of bombings, kidnappings, assassinations and economic pressure have sharply reduced that number, with many Christians leaving for neighboring countries or the West.

Iraqi officials said security forces had been deployed to Christian neighborhoods in Mosul and along routes used by displaced families. Authorities announced arrests and promised protection, but many Christians said they had little confidence that the state could guarantee their safety.

The intimidation in Mosul comes as Iraq continues to face scattered extremist attacks despite an overall decline in violence from the worst years of sectarian war. Al Qaeda in Iraq, which rose to prominence after 2003 and became notorious for suicide bombings, sectarian massacres and attacks on religious minorities, has been under pressure from U.S.-backed Sunni militias and Iraqi security forces. But the group has retained the ability to carry out assassinations and bombings, particularly in northern Iraq.

In Baghdad, additional attacks underscored the continuing insecurity. Bombings and shootings have struck civilian areas, including neighborhoods where minority communities remain exposed. Christian churches and institutions in the capital have been repeatedly targeted in past years, contributing to a steady flight of Christians from Baghdad and other cities.

Farther north and west, violence has also hit Tal Afar, a predominantly Turkmen city near the Syrian border that has seen repeated insurgent attacks and sectarian killings. Bombings there have targeted markets, security forces and residential areas, reflecting the broader instability across Nineveh province.

The Mosul crisis has drawn appeals from church officials and human rights advocates, who warned that continued attacks could erase a community whose roots in the region stretch back nearly two millennia. Some leaders called on the Iraqi government to create better local protection forces for minority areas, while others urged international assistance for displaced families.

For those who fled, the immediate question is whether they can safely return. Many left with only what they could carry, locking doors behind them without knowing whether their homes would be looted or seized. Shop owners abandoned businesses; students missed school; families crowded into church halls and unfinished buildings.

“We left because we were afraid,” one displaced resident said. “When people are killed because they are Christian, what choice do we have?”

The violence in Mosul highlights a persistent challenge for Iraq: even as national security indicators improve, vulnerable minorities remain at risk in places where insurgents, criminal gangs and political rivalries overlap. For Christians in northern Iraq, the latest threats have deepened a sense that their future in the country is increasingly uncertain.
